go:523036.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 1 | Question: 44
go:523036.question:
Consider a system that has a cache memory unit and a memory management unit (MMU). The address input to the cache memory is a physical address. The MMU has a translation lookaside buffer (TLB). Assume that when a page is evicted from the main memory, the corresponding blocks in the cache are marked as invalid.

For a given memory reference, which of the following sequences of events can NEVER happen?

  1. TLB miss, Page table hit, Cache hit
  2. TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit
  3. TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit
  4. TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache miss

detailed_solution.markdown: A memory reference passes through, in order: TLB → (page table, only if TLB misses) → cache. - TLB miss, Page table hit, Cache hit: possible — TLB doesn't have the mapping, page table does (page is in memory), and the corresponding cache block (whose validity depends on the page being resident) can indeed be valid and hit. Can happen. - TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit: impossible. A TLB hit means the page is currently mapped/resident in memory (TLB entries are only valid for pages currently in memory); it is therefore contradictory for the page table to then report a miss (page not in memory) for that very same page. - TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit: impossible. A page-table miss means the page is not in main memory at all — and the problem states that when a page is evicted, its cache blocks are marked invalid. So if the page isn't in memory, its cache blocks cannot be valid, and a cache hit is impossible. - TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache miss: possible and in fact the expected/consistent sequence when a page is genuinely not resident.

go:523035.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 1 | Question: 45
go:523035.question:
An undirected, unweighted, simple graph $G(V, E)$ is said to be $2$-colorable if there exists a function $c: V \rightarrow\{0,1\}$ such that for every $(u, v) \in E, c(u) \neq c(v)$.

Which of the following statements about $2$-colorable graphs is/are true?

  1. If $G$ is $2$-colorable, then $G$ may contain cycles of odd length
  2. If $G$ is $2$-colorable, then $G$ may contain cycles of even length
  3. An optimal algorithm for testing whether $G$ is $2$-colorable runs in time $\Theta(|V|+|E|)$, if $G$ is represented as an adjacency list
  4. An optimal algorithm for testing whether $G$ is $2$-colorable runs in time $\Theta(|E| \log |V|)$, if $G$ is represented as an adjacency list

detailed_solution.markdown: A graph is $2$-colorable if and only if it is bipartite, which is exactly equivalent to having no odd-length cycle. - "May contain cycles of odd length" — false, a 2-colorable graph can never contain an odd cycle (that's precisely the bipartiteness characterization). - "May contain cycles of even length" — true, even cycles are perfectly fine in a bipartite graph (e.g. alternating the two colors around the cycle works exactly when the cycle length is even). - Algorithm complexity: Testing bipartiteness/$2$-colorability is done via a single BFS or DFS traversal, alternately coloring each vertex as it's visited and checking for conflicts — this runs in $\Theta(|V|+|E|)$ time on an adjacency-list representation, and this is optimal since you must at least look at every vertex and edge once. True. - $\Theta(|E|\log|V|)$ is not the optimal/typical complexity for this simple traversal-based check (that bound is more associated with, e.g., priority-queue-based MST/shortest-path algorithms), so this is false as a claim about the optimal algorithm for 2-colorability testing.

go:523034.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 1 | Question: 46
go:523034.question:
An ISP having an address block $202.16.0.0/15$ assigns a block of $6000$ IP addresses to a client, using the classless internet domain routing (CIDR) super-netting approach. Which of the following address blocks can be assigned by the ISP?

  1. $202.16.0.0/19$
  2. $202.17.64.0/19$
  3. $202.16.32.0/19$
  4. $202.17.24.0/19$

detailed_solution.markdown: The ISP's block $202.16.0.0/15$ spans two full class-B-sized blocks: all addresses from $202.16.0.0$ to $202.17.255.255$. For $6000$ addresses via CIDR super-netting, we need a block with at least $6000$ addresses; a $/19$ prefix gives $2^{32-19}=2^{13}=8192$ addresses, which suffices (a $/20$ would only give $4096<6000$). A valid $/19$ sub-block must (a) lie entirely within $202.16.0.0$-$202.17.255.255$, and (b) have its network address aligned to a multiple of $32$ in the relevant octet (since $/19$ leaves $13$ host bits, and $2^{13}=8192=32\times256$ addresses per block, so the 3rd octet must be a multiple of $32$: $0,32,64,\ldots$). - $202.16.0.0/19$: $0$ is a valid multiple of $32$, and within range. Valid. - $202.17.64.0/19$: $64$ is a valid multiple of $32$, $202.17.x$ is within the /15 range. Valid. - $202.16.32.0/19$: $32$ is a valid multiple of $32$. Valid. - $202.17.24.0/19$: $24$ is not a multiple of $32$ (valid boundaries are $0,32,64,\ldots$), so this is not a properly aligned $/19$ block. Invalid.

go:523033.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 1 | Question: 47
go:523033.question: Let $G$ be an undirected graph, which is a path on $8$ vertices. The number of matchings in $G$ is $\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: Let $f(k)$ denote the number of matchings (including the empty matching) in a path graph with $k$ edges. Considering the last edge of the path: either it is not used in the matching (leaving $f(k-1)$ choices for the rest), or it is used (which forbids the adjacent edge, leaving $f(k-2)$ choices for the rest). This gives the Fibonacci-like recurrence: $f(k)=f(k-1)+f(k-2)$, with $f(0)=1$ (no edges: only the empty matching) and $f(1)=2$ (one edge: either included or not). $f(2)=3,\ f(3)=5,\ f(4)=8,\ f(5)=13,\ f(6)=21,\ f(7)=34$. A path on $8$ vertices has $7$ edges, so the number of matchings is $f(7)=34$.

go:523032.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 1 | Question: 48
go:523032.question:
Let $X$ be a random variable which takes values in the set $\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8\}$. Further, $\operatorname{Pr}(X=1)=\operatorname{Pr}(X=2)=\operatorname{Pr}(X=5)=\operatorname{Pr}(X=7)=\frac{1}{6}$ and $\operatorname{Pr}(X=3)=\operatorname{Pr}(X=4)=\operatorname{Pr}(X=6)=\operatorname{Pr}(X=8)=\frac{1}{12}$.

The expected value of $X$, denoted by $E[X]$, is equal to $\_\_\_\_$. (rounded off to two decimal places)

detailed_solution.markdown:
$E[X]=\sum x\cdot\Pr(X=x)$

$=\left(1+2+5+7\right)\times\dfrac{1}{6}+\left(3+4+6+8\right)\times\dfrac{1}{12}$

$=15\times\dfrac{1}{6}+21\times\dfrac{1}{12}$

$=2.5+1.75=4.25$

go:523031.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 1 | Question: 49
go:523031.question:
Consider a hard disk with a rotational speed of $15000$ rpm. The time to move the read/write head from a track to its adjacent track is $1$ millisecond. Initially, the head is on track $0$. The number of sectors per track is $400$. The sector size is $1024$ bytes. It is necessary to transfer data from $10$ randomly located sectors in each of the following tracks in the order: $5, 12$ and $7$.

The total time for the data transfer (in milliseconds) from the hard disk is $\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$. (rounded off to one decimal place)

detailed_solution.markdown: Rotation time per revolution $=\dfrac{60000\text{ ms}}{15000}=4$ ms, so average rotational latency (half a revolution) $=2$ ms, and time per sector $=\dfrac{4\text{ ms}}{400\text{ sectors}}=0.01$ ms. Seek time (head moves $1$ ms per adjacent track, following the path $0\to5\to12\to7$): $0\to5$: $5$ tracks $=5$ ms; $5\to12$: $7$ tracks $=7$ ms; $12\to7$: $5$ tracks $=5$ ms. Total seek $=5+7+5=17$ ms. Data transfer per track: since the $10$ sectors needed are randomly located, each individual sector access requires (on average) a fresh rotational latency of $2$ ms before the required sector arrives under the head, plus the $0.01$ ms to actually read it: Per track $=10\times(2+0.01)=20.1$ ms. Over $3$ tracks: $3\times20.1=60.3$ ms. Total time $=$ seek $+$ transfer $=17+60.3=77.3$ ms.

go:523030.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 1 | Question: 50
go:523030.question:
The EX stage of a pipelined processor performs the memory read operations for LOAD instructions, and the operations for the arithmetic and logic instructions. Let $t_{E X}$ denote the time taken by the EX stage to perform the operation for an instruction. For each instruction type, the values of $t_{E X}$ and $M$ (the number of instructions of that type in a sequence of $100$ instructions for a program P ), are given in the table below.

The duration of the pipeline clock cycle is $1$ nanosecond. Assume that the latch time for the interstage buffers in the pipeline is negligible.

\[
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{array}{|l|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Instruction} &
\begin{array}{c}
t_{EX}\ \text{in} \\
\text{nanoseconds}
\end{array}
& M \\
\hline
\text{LOAD} & 1.8 & 15 \\
\hline
\text{IMUL} & 1.5 & 10 \\
\hline
\text{IDIV} & 2.5 & 5 \\
\hline
\text{FADD} & 1.7 & 10 \\
\hline
\text{FSUB} & 1.7 & 5 \\
\hline
\text{FMUL} & 2.8 & 15 \\
\hline
\text{FDIV} & 3.2 & 5 \\
\hline
\begin{array}{l}
\text{All other} \\
\text{instructions}
\end{array}
&
\begin{array}{c}
\text{Less than} \\
1.0
\end{array}
& 35 \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]
When program $\text{P}$ is executed, the number of clock cycles for which the pipeline is stalled due to structural hazards in the EX stage is $\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown:
There is a single, shared EX-stage functional unit; only one instruction can occupy the EX stage per clock cycle (of duration $1$ ns). If an instruction's actual execution time $t_{EX}$ exceeds $1$ ns, it must occupy the EX stage for $\lceil t_{EX}\rceil$ clock cycles, causing $\left(\lceil t_{EX}\rceil-1\right)$ structural-hazard stall cycles for every instance of that instruction type.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c}\text{Type}&t_{EX}&\text{cycles needed}&\text{stalls}\times M\\\hline\text{LOAD}&1.8&2&1\times15=15\\\text{IMUL}&1.5&2&1\times10=10\\\text{IDIV}&2.5&3&2\times5=10\\\text{FADD}&1.7&2&1\times10=10\\\text{FSUB}&1.7&2&1\times5=5\\\text{FMUL}&2.8&3&2\times15=30\\\text{FDIV}&3.2&4&3\times5=15\\\text{Others}&{<}1.0&1&0\times35=0\end{array}$$

Total stall cycles $=15+10+10+10+5+30+15+0=95$.

go:523029.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 1 | Question: 51
go:523029.question:
Consider the recursive functions represented by the following code segment:

int bar(int n) {
    if (n == 1) return 0;
    else return 1 + bar(n/2);
}
int foo(int n) {
    if (n == 1) return 1;
    else return 1 + foo(bar(n));
}

The smallest positive integer n for which $\mathrm{f} \circ \circ(\mathrm{n})$ returns $5$ is $\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

Note: Ignore syntax errors (if any) in the function.

detailed_solution.markdown: First, note $\text{bar}(n)$ repeatedly integer-halves $n$ until reaching $1$, counting the number of halvings — this is exactly $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$. $\text{foo}(n)=1+\text{foo}(\text{bar}(n))$ for $n>1$, and $\text{foo}(1)=1$. So $\text{foo}(n)$ counts $1$ plus the number of times we must apply $\text{bar}$ (i.e. take $\lfloor\log_2\cdot\rfloor$) starting from $n$ to eventually reach $1$. Build up the smallest $n$ achieving each target value of $\text{foo}$: - $\text{foo}(n)=1$: smallest $n=1$. - $\text{foo}(n)=2$: need $\text{bar}(n)=1$, i.e. $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor=1$: smallest $n=2$. - $\text{foo}(n)=3$: need $\text{bar}(n)=2$: smallest $n=2^2=4$. - $\text{foo}(n)=4$: need $\text{bar}(n)=4$: smallest $n=2^4=16$. - $\text{foo}(n)=5$: need $\text{bar}(n)=16$: smallest $n=2^{16}=65536$.

go:523028.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 1 | Question: 52
go:523028.question:
The following sequence corresponds to the preorder traversal of a binary search tree $T$ :
\[
50,25,13,40,30,47,75,60,70,80,77
\]
The position of the element $60$ in the postorder traversal of $T$ is $\_\_\_\_$ . (answer in integer)

Note: The position begins with $1$.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Reconstruct the BST from the preorder $50,25,13,40,30,47,75,60,70,80,77$ (each root's left subtree holds smaller values, right subtree holds larger values, read off in preorder root-first fashion):

$50$ is the root. Left subtree (values $<50$): $25,13,40,30,47$; right subtree (values $>50$): $75,60,70,80,77$.

Left subtree: root $25$, left child $13$ (leaf), right subtree $40,30,47$ → root $40$, left $30$, right $47$.

Right subtree: root $75$, left subtree $60,70$ → root $60$ with right child $70$ (no left); right subtree $80,77$ → root $80$ with left child $77$ (no right).

Postorder (left, right, root) of the whole tree:

From the $25$-subtree: $13,\ 30,47,40,\ 25$

From the $75$-subtree: $70,60,\ 77,80,\ 75$

Then the root $50$.

Full postorder: $13,\,30,\,47,\,40,\,25,\,70,\,60,\,77,\,80,\,75,\,50$

Counting positions (starting at $1$): $60$ is the $7$th element.

go:523027.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 1 | Question: 53
go:523027.question:
Consider the following program snippet. Assume that the program compiles and runs successfully. Further, assume that the fork() system call is always successful in creating a process.

int main () {
    int i;
    for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        if (fork() == 0) {
            continue;
        }
        break;
    }
    printf("Hello!");
    return 0;
}

The total number of times that the printf statement gets executed is $\_\_\_\_$. (answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: Trace the loop, remembering that after $\text{fork()}$, the child gets return value $0$ (executes $\text{continue}$, moving to the next loop iteration), while the parent gets a nonzero value (executes $\text{break}$, immediately leaving the loop). - $i=0$: original process forks → parent breaks immediately (1 process reaches printf with $i=0$); the child continues the loop. - $i=1$ (in that child): it forks again → this process (now acting as parent of its own fork) breaks (2nd process reaches printf); its own child continues. - $i=2$ (in that grandchild): forks again → this one breaks (3rd process reaches printf); its child continues. - $i=3$ (in the great-grandchild): loop condition $i<3$ fails, so the loop ends naturally without another fork (4th process reaches printf). So exactly $4$ distinct processes each execute the $\text{printf}$ statement exactly once.

go:523026.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 1 | Question: 54
go:523026.question: Consider a CPU that has to execute two types of processes. The first type, Actuators (A), requires a CPU burst of $6$ seconds. The second type, Controllers (C), requires a CPU burst of $8$ seconds. A new process of type A arrives at time $t=10$, $20, 30, 40$, and $50$ (in seconds). Similarly, a new process of type C arrives at time $t=$ $11, 22, 33, 44$, and $55$ (in seconds). The CPU scheduling policy is First Come First Serve (FCFS). The first process of type A starts running at $t=10$ seconds. The average waiting time (in seconds) for the $10$ processes is $\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$. (rounded off to one decimal place)

detailed_solution.markdown:
List all $10$ arrivals in chronological order and simulate FCFS execution (CPU serves strictly in arrival order, non-preemptive):

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}\text{Proc}&\text{Arrival}&\text{Burst}&\text{Start}&\text{Finish}&\text{Waiting}\\\hline A&10&6&10&16&0\\C&11&8&16&24&5\\A&20&6&24&30&4\\C&22&8&30&38&8\\A&30&6&38&44&8\\C&33&8&44&52&11\\A&40&6&52&58&12\\C&44&8&58&66&14\\A&50&6&66&72&16\\C&55&8&72&80&17\end{array}$$

Sum of waiting times $=0+5+4+8+8+11+12+14+16+17=95$.

Average waiting time $=\dfrac{95}{10}=9.5$ seconds.

go:523025.title: GATE CSE 2026 | Set 1 | Question: 55
go:523025.question: Consider a relational database schema with a relation $R(A, B, C, D)$. If $\{A, B\}$ and $\{A, C\}$ are the only two candidate keys of the relation $R$, then the number of superkeys of relation $R$ is $\_\_\_\_$.  (answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: A superkey is any subset of attributes that contains at least one candidate key as a subset. Here the $4$ attributes are $\{A,B,C,D\}$ and the candidate keys are $\{A,B\}$ and $\{A,C\}$. Count subsets of $\{A,B,C,D\}$ containing $\{A,B\}$: freely choose the remaining $\{C,D\}$ → $2^2=4$ subsets. Count subsets containing $\{A,C\}$: freely choose the remaining $\{B,D\}$ → $2^2=4$ subsets. Subsets counted twice are those containing both $\{A,B\}$ and $\{A,C\}$, i.e. containing $\{A,B,C\}$: freely choose remaining $\{D\}$ → $2^1=2$ subsets. By inclusion-exclusion, total superkeys $=4+4-2=6$.
